page_header_content.content: Review of the Papua New Guinea Tariff Reduction Programme

paragraph_content.content: Papua New Guinea embarked on the Tariff Reduction Programme (TRP) as part of a broader economic recovery and reform agenda that aimed to improve economic efficiency and integrate with global markets. By 2015, Papua New Guinea's tariffs were at historic lows, around 3.2 per cent on average, making it one of the most open economies in the region. After further tariff reductions, the government suspended the final stage of tariff cuts in 2018. It progressively raised tariffs on some products, citing the need to protect infant industries and boost revenue. As Papua New Guinea implements new national development frameworks, including the Papua New Guinea National Trade Policy 2017–2032, the Medium-Term Development Plan IV (2023–2027), and the Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (2023–2027), as well as other sector-specific plans in fisheries, forestry, agriculture, and manufacturing, there is a need for a structured and evidence-based assessment of the TRP.

This report provides a review of Papua New Guinea's TRP from 2010 to the present, examining its chronology and phases, the policy rationale for both liberalisation and reversal, and the impacts. To evaluate the outcomes and impacts of the TRP, the study relies on two complementary methodologies: an ex-post econometric analysis of trade flows, which assesses the results of the implementation of the TRP on specific economic variables, and an ex-ante partial equilibrium simulation, which evaluates the expected changes to occur as a result of tariff changes on trade flows, tariff revenue, sectoral impacts, consumer welfare, and other broader business impacts, holding all other variables constant. The analysis focuses on two periods for comparisons: TRP phase 2 (2012-2017) and the TRP suspension (2018-2023). To supplement the quantitative analysis of the TRP impact assessment, stakeholder consultations, in the form of a survey, were conducted with national government agencies, business associations, and companies to identify the perceived benefits, challenges, and recommendations for future measures to support Papua New Guinea firms in building competitiveness.

On tariff outcomes, the review highlights a policy shift from liberalization to selective protectionism. During the TRP, tariffs declined across all product categories, with consumer goods falling from 6.4 to 5.2 per cent, raw materials from 11.4 to 10.8 per cent, intermediates from 2 to 1.5 per cent, and capital goods near zero. This period also saw reduced dispersion of rates, leading to a simpler tariff schedule. However, after the TRP's suspension in 2018, tariffs moderately increased, with consumer goods rising to 5.3 per cent and raw materials to 11.3 per cent (both in simple average terms), reflecting renewed protection for targeted industries. By 2023, tariffs signalled support for infant industries, but overall dispersion was more rationalized than in 2010. This policy volatility created uncertainty: 61 per cent of surveyed firms reported that tariff revisions between 2018-2020 disrupted investment decisions. While the overall trend of moving from broad liberalization to selective protectionism aimed to foster domestic industries and reduce import dependence, it may come at the cost of higher consumer prices, complex trade-offs for firms, and weaker competitiveness if uncertainty persists.

On economic outcomes and sectoral impacts, the TRP coincided with a period of reduced import demand. Therefore, Papua New Guinea did not experience an import surge, linked to the lowering of tariffs. Instead, it benefited from strong export earnings coming from mining and petroleum. When Papua New Guinea reversed course and raised tariffs in 2018, the tariff hikes had a limited additional dampening effect on import levels, which had already been low and stable. Overall, Papua New Guinea's economy overall exhibited remarkable gross domestic product (GDP) growth averaging 6.3 per cent annually during the active TRP period, compared to the post-suspension period growth of two per cent. It is, however, important to consider multiple factors that contributed to the differential trends, including global commodity cycles and major resource project developments (for the TRP), as well as the COVID-19 outbreak (for the TRP suspension phase). The gravity model's findings support the conventional wisdom that tariff increases yield a reduction in imports: model runs on data during 2012-2023 showed that a 1 per cent increase in tariffs (ad valorem) is associated with roughly a 2.1 per cent decrease in import value on average. The partial equilibrium findings showed single-digit millions of dollars change in imports for major partners (e.g. a $6.8 million drop in imports from China due to post-2018 tariff hikes), reinforcing the notion that other factors overshadowed the tariff policy in determining Papua New Guinea's trade volumes.

On tariff revenue, tariff policy plays an important but diminishing role in Papua New Guinea's fiscal revenue. The tax-to-GDP ratio declined to 15.8 per cent in 2023, even as tax revenue grew in absolute terms. Import duties rose from $71.5 million in 2010 to $112 million in 2023,

yet their share in total revenue fell as the Global Sales Tax and other taxes became more prominent. Consumer goods remain the largest source of tariff revenue because of high import volumes, especially for fuel, vehicles, alcohol, and tobacco. In contrast, raw materials and intermediates generate little revenue despite some high nominal rates, due to low import volumes. Simulations indicate tariff cuts during the TRP (2012–2017) reduced revenue by only about $7.8 million annually, or just one per cent of tariff revenue, a negligible effect. After 2018, tariff hikes were expected to boost revenue, but collections were about $15.6 million lower than they would have been under 2018 baseline tariffs. This outcome was driven largely by the sharp cut in tobacco duties, one of Papua New Guinea's top revenue sources, alongside reduced import volumes and likely evasion incentives. The experience showed tariff liberalization cost Papua New Guinea little in revenue terms.

Industry views, as expressed through the business survey, paint a complex picture of competitive challenges that are informative for trade policy considerations beyond direct tariff impacts on trade flows. During the TRP, 36 per cent of firms reported benefits from tariff reductions through lower input costs, enabling price cuts, expansion, and productivity gains, though 55 per cent saw no impact. After tariff increases from 2018, 53 per cent of firms reported negative effects, suggesting policy volatility created winners and losers, with losses more visible than gains. Import competition was reportedly intensified, with 53 per cent of firms reporting impacts on sales and business models due to consumer preferences for cheaper imports. Price is perceived as the main problem: Papua New Guinea businesses were concerned that they cannot match import prices because their costs (transport, electricity, inputs) are too high. Next to price consideration, quality perception emerged as the second most important factor affecting competitiveness, per Papua New Guinea businesses' perception. Businesses further identified transport and logistics costs among the most severe constraints, alongside expensive inputs, policy unpredictability, and regulatory burdens. These findings show Papua New Guinea's competitive challenges are structural and require supportive infrastructure and regulatory reforms alongside trade policy.

Innovation under this report is considered broadly via the ability to introduce new products to the market. During the TRP, Papua New Guinea experienced a notable surge in export diversification, followed by a decline once tariffs were raised. Between 2010 and 2018, the number of distinct export products expanded significantly, with 591 new products entering Papua New Guinea's export portfolio, representing 45 per cent of the total basket. However, the majority of these exported items were of low value, with only 44 new products exceeding $100,000 in value in 2018. This latest export drive was supported by cheaper imported inputs and machinery, which lowered production costs and enabled firms to test new product lines in international markets. However, sustainability was limited, with only 465 products (35 per cent) surviving through the period, underscoring the importance of addressing structural constraints beyond tariff reductions.

paragraph_content.content: Consumer welfare was affected by the radical change in tariffs of a few product groups. During 2010–2018, simulations show a net welfare loss of around $5.9 million for Papua New Guinea consumers. While tariffs fell on many consumer goods, Papua New Guinea retained or raised very high tariffs on beverages and tobacco, which alone caused losses of about $6.5 million. Beyond beverages and tobacco products, Papua New Guinea increased tariffs on about $390 million of other goods, lifting average rates from 5 to 14 per cent which contributes a welfare loss of $1 million. The total consumer welfare loss, therefore, outweighed the $1.6 million gain consumers enjoyed from all the other tariff reductions.

The evidence reveals that tariff policy alone cannot determine economic development outcomes in contexts where structural constraints fundamentally limit competitiveness. Papua New Guinea's businesses face transport costs, energy expenses, and regulatory complexity that often dwarf the effects of tariff modifications, suggesting that successful development strategies must also address these underlying constraints to deliver more results from trade policy instruments like tariffs.

Yet trade policy remains an important component of the government policy toolbox for a comprehensive development strategy. The TRP period's correlation with stronger economic growth, export diversification, and increased business dynamism suggests that trade openness can contribute to economic vitality when implemented within supportive policy frameworks. Conversely, contraction in exports and GDP following TRP suspension appears to show some association between the two.

The study of the TRP reveals both potential benefits and limitations of trade policy as a development tool, which provide valuable lessons for future policy design and implementation. It is suggested that to yield results, trade policy requires consistent efforts to address fundamental constraints while maintaining openness to international opportunities that can accelerate development progress. Moving forward, Papua New Guinea should aim to formulate a tariff policy that balances development objectives with fiscal revenue needs and a realistic dependence on outside sourcing for its industry.
The following recommendations are suggested for future tariff policy formulation:
Restore gradual tariff rationalization

paragraph_content.content: Papua New Guinea should adopt a predictable, phased tariff reduction path to allow industries time to adjust. A simpler, more uniform structure with low rates would reduce distortions, improve certainty, and avoid counterproductive high tariffs that harm consumers, encourage smuggling, and undermine industrial growth.

Policy should prioritize reducing the high cost of doing business rather than shielding firms with tariffs. Investments in infrastructure, power supply, and streamlined customs can lower costs, while reducing tariffs on key inputs will directly enhance competitiveness and help firms produce goods that can compete globally.

title_content.content: 3. Use targeted support for infant industries

paragraph_content.content: Support to priority sectors should be time-bound, specific, and performance-based rather than relying on broad tariff protection. Targeted measures like subsidies, tax relief, or technical assistance will boost productivity and encourage industries to mature into competitive sectors, while public-private dialogue can ensure support meets actual business needs.

title_content.content: 4. Safeguard consumer welfare and food security

paragraph_content.content: Tariff policy must protect low-income households by keeping tariffs on essential goods like food, fuel, and medicine at low or zero rates. Excise taxes, rather than tariffs, should be used to regulate socially harmful goods such as alcohol and tobacco without distorting trade or raising consumer costs unfairly.

Beyond lowering tariffs, Papua New Guinea should reduce non-tariff barriers and strengthen customs efficiency to lower trade costs. Greater engagement in regional and multilateral agreements, such as PACER Plus, MSG, ASEAN+1, and WTO initiatives, can expand market access, improve input sourcing, and support diversification of export opportunities.

Tariff policy should follow a transparent, institutionalized review process rather than ad hoc budget announcements. Establishing a Tariff Advisory Board and conducting regular impact assessments would help ensure tariff measures are evidence-based, predictable, and phased out when no longer needed, boosting investor confidence and policy credibility.

Papua New Guinea should build institutional capacity to monitor, investigate, and respond to unfair trade practices such as dumping or subsidised exports. Enacting anti-dumping and safeguard laws, supported by a specialised trade remedies unit, would help protect domestic industries, maintain a level playing field, and align with WTO rules.

paragraph_content.content:
Chapter 1
Introduction

Papua New Guinea rolled out the Tariff Reduction Programme (TRP) in 1999 as part of a broader economic recovery and reform agenda. After a phase of deep tariff cuts, which started in 2012, the TRP was suspended in 2018 with the reversing of rates for some tariff lines. As Papua New Guinea implement new national development frameworks, including the Papua New Guinea National Trade Policy 2017–2032, the Medium-Term Development Plan IV (2023–2027), and the Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (2023–2027), as well as other sector-specific plans in fisheries, forestry, agriculture, and manufacturing, there is a need for a structured and evidence-based assessment of the TRP.

This TRP review is intended to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the cost and benefits of the TRP to date, assess the economic implications of its suspension, and provide well-informed policy options for the future. This includes determining the TRP's impact on domestic industries, consumers, trade competitiveness, and alignment with international agreements such as the Interim Economic Partnership Agreement (iEPA) with the European Union and commitments under regional and multilateral frameworks.
This study meets several specific objectives as follows:

- To evaluate the impact of tariff changes on the private sector, including determining effects on competitiveness, efficiency and productivity by surveying companies to understand their response to the policy.

• To analyse the benefits and costs of tariff changes on different stakeholders, including consumers (through choice/variety of products and price reductions), businesses (competitiveness), and trade participants (importers/exporters).
- To determine the impact of tariff changes supporting downstream processing and value addition in sectors such as manufacturing, fisheries, and agriculture.
- To evaluate whether certain exogenous factors explain any unintended outcomes arising from the tariff changes.

The review provides a set of conclusions and recommendations in order to guide the development of a future coherent, transparent, and development-friendly import tariff policy that supports the government's overarching objectives of promoting value addition, import substitution, and economic resilience in a globally competitive context.

paragraph_content.content:
Chapter 2
Context

Papua New Guinea is a lower-middle-income economy with a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of $32.8 billion and GDP per capita of $2.6 thousand in 2025 (IMF, 2025). This income level is modest by global standards and also below the East Asia and Pacific averages of $3.6 thousand. The Papua New Guinea economy has been on a positive growth trajectory since

2000, with episodes of negative growth due to low commodity prices (early 2000s), financial crisis (2008), the end of the liquefied natural gas (LNG)-led construction boom (2018), and the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2021) (ADB, 2012; IMF, 2025). Post-pandemic, the country managed to achieve stable growth of around 4-5 per cent annually (see Figure 1).
The Papua New Guinea economy has been on a positive growth trajectory since 2000

paragraph_content.content: Extractive industries (minerals, petroleum) and agriculture form the backbone of Papua New Guinea's economy. According to data from the Papua New Guinea National Statistical Office (2025), Mining and Quarrying contributed to 27 per cent of the national gross output in 2022, followed by Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing (15 per cent), and Construction (9 per cent). Meanwhile, manufacturing and broader industrial sectors remain small, accounting for 5 per cent of the national gross output in 2022. This narrow production base means growth surges during commodity booms (or project construction phases) but also leaves Papua New Guinea vulnerable to global price swings and incidental shocks.

Mining, after an initial decline from 2010 to 2012, saw a significant surge from 2014 to 2019, followed by a further surge in 2021–22, in line with the global commodity boom and Papua New Guinea's increased mineral exports. Manufacturing, on the other hand, did not grow as quickly as agriculture and mining until 2020 but then expanded strongly between 2021 and 2023.

Exchange rate developments during this period were influenced by capital inflows associated with the construction phase of a large liquefied natural gas project, which led to a marked appreciation of the kina in real terms up to around 2012 (IMF, 2015). Following the completion of the construction phase, the real effective exchange rate remained at a higher level and has since fluctuated within a relatively narrow range (Figure 2). This sustained high real effective exchange rate has implications for international competitiveness, as it makes exports relatively more expensive and imports relatively cheaper than domestically produced goods, all else being equal.

Over 20 years, Papua New Guinea's ranking in economic complexity has drifted downward, indicating that it is not moving much into new, higher-capability products. Furthermore, product specialization remained limited. During 2010-2023, Papua New Guinea's product space has remained concentrated on some products in the Minerals and Agriculture clusters (Figure 4).

The concentration in low- to moderate-complexity commodities gives Papua New Guinea certain characteristics –namely, vulnerability to commodity price swings, but also strong export revenues when prices rise. However, this structure limits Papua New Guinea's ability to move up the value chain, develop export products with greater technology, branding, or processing content, and thus capture more value. Because many of its current comparative advantages are in goods that require fewer complementary capabilities (infrastructure, advanced skills, industrial inputs), moving into more complex products will require building those capabilities.

Diversification is similarly constrained by the geography of Papua New Guinea's product space: many products that are adjacent (i.e. “nearby” in the product space) to what Papua New Guinea currently exports are still commodities or low-processed goods (e.g. further processing of minerals or agricultural goods). There appear to be few “low-hanging fruit” opportunities in high-tech or knowledge-intensive manufacturing already very close to Papua New Guinea’s existing export basket. The product space suggests that Papua New Guinea must invest in capabilities (skilled labour, reliable infrastructure, regulatory capacity) to bridge larger “distances” in the product space for diversification. Innovation (in terms of product design, new export categories) will likely come slowly unless there is sustained policy effort toward human capital, research and development (R&D), value-added processing, and connectivity both domestically and with international value chains.

The evidence from 20 resource-rich economies suggests that resource-rich countries tend to exhibit a relatively constant level of economic complexity, with limited progress. Some explanations for this observation are that the findings of the study support the natural resource curse hypothesis, confirming that countries rich in natural resources tend to have lower economic complexity. Additionally, the study highlights the positive impact of corruption control on economic complexity, indicating that improving good governance can contribute to the improvement of economic complexity in resource-rich countries (Owjimehr & Jamshidi, 2024).

title_content.content: B. Papua New Guinea's Tariff Reduction Programme: a chronology
1. Initiation of the Tariff Reduction Programme (late 1990s – early 2000s)

paragraph_content.content: Papua New Guinea embarked on a significant Tariff Reduction Programme (TRP) in 1999 as part of a broader economic recovery and reform agenda. The TRP was introduced in exchange for support from international financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank, and was aimed at making Papua New Guinea's trade regime more open and competitive (Scollay, 2007). A new Value Added Tax (VAT) and Government Sales Tax (GST) were simultaneously implemented to offset the revenue losses from cutting tariffs. The government's 1997 Tariff Reform White Paper, inspired by a 1996 World Bank review, argued that high import duties were hindering efficiency, raising business costs, and protecting uncompetitive industries. Lowering tariffs was seen as a way to encourage a more productive private sector by exposing firms to international competition. At the same time, the new VAT would replace tariffs as a revenue source (Scollay, 2007). This policy shift came at a time of economic difficulty, following the Asian financial crisis and commodity price slumps of the late 1990s, but reflected Papua New Guinea's commitment to outward-oriented reforms under World Trade Organisation (WTO) membership and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) goals.

Under the TRP, Papua New Guinea simplified its tariff structure and implemented gradual cuts between 1999-2006. Tariffs on goods produced locally, approximately three-quarters of all imports, were set to zero, making most products duty-free (Scollay, 2007). All remaining imported goods (those produced domestically or with production potential in Papua New Guinea) were classified into three tariff bands: “intermediate” (30 per cent), “protective” (40 per cent), and “prohibitive” (55 per cent) rates.

The TRP legislated stepwise reductions of 5 percentage points for each band at set intervals. In practice, tariffs fell in stages on January 1 of 1999, 2000, 2001, 2003, and finally 2006. By the end of 2006, the intermediate rate had been reduced to 15 per cent, the protective rate to 25 per cent, and the prohibitive rate to 40 per cent.

These cuts effectively halved Papua New Guinea's average applied tariff, with the unweighted average tariff dropping from about 20 per cent in the late 1990s to roughly 5 per cent by 2006. The new structure dramatically increased the share of duty-free lines from around 3 per cent before the cuts, to about 77 per cent of tariff lines by 2006. Only about 15 per cent of tariff lines (mainly for domestically produced foods and manufactures) still faced import duties at the protective 25 per cent or prohibitive 40 per cent rates by 2006 (UNCTAD, 2006). A few sensitive products, such as sugar, canned fish, salt, tobacco, alcohol, and plywood, had been granted special high protection due to prior government commitments or industry

Overall, the first phase of the TRP (1999-2006) achieved a more open trade regime with a simpler, lower tariff structure, aligning Papua New Guinea's policies closer to global norms and its WTO bindings.

The rapid tariff reductions in the early 2000s generated controversy. On the one hand, the reform was praised for improving efficiency and lowering costs; on the other, domestic manufacturers grew concerned about increased competition (Fox et al., 2018; Laveil, 2020). By 2002-2003, evidence suggested that government revenue had fallen more than expected due to lower economic activities, particularly declining mineral revenue, and less revenue from tariffs (UNCTAD, 2006). These fiscal pressures and industry concerns led to calls to slow down or modify the TRP. In 2003, the Manufacturers' Council of Papua New Guinea petitioned the government to suspend further tariff cuts, proposing to freeze rates at 45, 30, and 20 per cent (instead of dropping to 40, 25, 15 per cent, as scheduled) (Scollay, 2007). In response, the government commissioned a Tariff Review Taskforce in 2003 to evaluate the impacts of the TRP. This review found that the tariff reductions did not negatively affect the economy nor devastate the manufacturing sector (Laveil, 2020). Notably, industries with the highest protective tariffs (such as canned tuna/mackerel processing) were among the slowest-growing, suggesting that heavy protection was not yielding the intended industrial growth (Laveil, 2020). High import duties were also found to affect exporters by raising the cost of imported inputs.

As a result of these findings, the government rejected the moratorium proposal and decided to complete the TRP as planned (Fox et al., 2018). By 2006, the final step of the initial program was implemented, bringing tariffs to their new low bands of 40, 25 and 15 per cent, as mentioned above. The 2003 review even recommended extending the tariff

cuts beyond 2006, envisioning further 5 per cent reductions every few years such that all tariffs would eventually converge at 15 per cent (Scollay, 2007; UNCTAD, 2006). However, this suggestion was not adopted at the time, and trade policy liberalization essentially paused once the first TRP was completed in 2006 (WTO, 2010). The mid-2000s debate underscored the balance Papua New Guinea sought between fostering infant industries and pursuing an open, competitive economy. While the government remained committed to outward-looking reform, it became clear that complementary measures (improving infrastructure, good governance, and tax compliance) were needed to maximize the benefits of tariff reform (Scollay, 2007).

While an independent review of the tariff policy suggested that lower tariffs were not causing damage to national industries and could support broader economic growth, many stakeholders remained unconvinced about the overall benefits arising from the tariff reductions. As a result, further tariff reforms were suspended.

After a brief pause in tariff changes, Papua New Guinea revisited its tariff policy to achieve further liberalisation in the late 2000s. The Tariff Review in 2007 (Scollay) assessed the post-TRP landscape and paved the way for a second phase of tariff reductions. The government's development strategies, such as the Medium-Term Development Strategy and Vision 2050/Development Strategic Plan, emphasizing improving competitiveness and integrating Papua New Guinea's economy with global and regional markets. In line with this, the 2007 review proposed additional gradual cuts to move Papua New Guinea toward a more uniform and lower tariff structure over the next decade (Fox et al., 2018). These recommendations were eventually codified in the Import and Export Customs Tariff Act of 2012, which legislated a schedule of tariff changes: some reductions took effect immediately in 2012, followed by further 5 per cent cuts planned on January 1, 2015, and again planned on January 1, 2018. The ultimate goal was to reduce the remaining protective tariffs to around 10 per cent, flattening the tariff bands at a low rate across all products by 2018 (Laveil, 2020). For example, under this plan, the standard protective duty rate would drop from 25 per cent (post-2006) down to 15 per cent by 2015 and 10 per cent by 2018, while the highest “prohibitive” rate would fall from 40 to 30 per cent by 2015 and eventually 25 per cent by 2018. By the mid-2010s, Papua New Guinea

Papua New Guinea's trade policy in this era remained outward-oriented, influenced by international commitments. As a member of the WTO, Papua New Guinea had bound many of its tariffs at ceilings (often around 40-45 per cent), and its applied rates after the TRP were well below these bindings (UNCTAD, 2006). This gave Papua New Guinea flexibility to liberalise and policy space to raise tariffs up to the bound rates if deemed necessary.
After a 2007 Tariff Review, it was recommended that further liberalisation be implemented toward a uniform, lower tariff structure:
- Protective tariffs dropped from 25 to 15 and then 10 per cent;
• Prohibitive tariffs from 40 to 30 and then 25 per cent by 2018;
• Average tariff bands declined from 42 (1999) to 18 per cent (2015).
Reforms were supported in the Medium-Term Development Strategy and Vision 2050 goals for competitiveness and global integration.

In terms of international commitments, WTO bindings at 40-45 per cent provided policy flexibility; APEC Bogor Goals endorsed free trade by 2020, and Papua New Guinea engaged in regional agreements (see Box 2).
Reductions were resumed and subsequently halted during this phase of the program. Overall, tariffs fell considerably.

title_content.content: Tariffs in the context of free trade agreements

paragraph_content.content: Papua New Guinea was also mindful of its regional and bilateral trade agreements. It joined the Pacific Island Countries Trade Agreement (effective mid-2000s) and the Melanesian Spearhead Group (MSG) agreement, which progressively eliminated tariffs on trade with neighbouring Pacific states, though these had a limited impact on overall tariff policy since they apply only to regional partners. Under an interim Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) with the European Union, signed in 2009 and ratified in 2011, Papua New Guinea committed to gradually fully liberalize 88 per cent of its imports from the European Union, with sensitive items excluded (European Commission, n.d.). Papua New Guinea chose to liberalise its trade with the European Union almost immediately, reflecting that many of those imports already faced low or zero most-favoured-nations (MFN) tariffs as a result of the TRP.

paragraph_content.content: Meanwhile, as an APEC member, Papua New Guinea had endorsed the Bogor Goals of free and open trade by 2020 for developing economies.

All these international frameworks reinforced Papua New Guinea's tariff reduction trajectory and the government's objective of using low, uniform tariffs to promote efficiency and investment. By 2015, tariffs were at historically low levels, and the country was more integrated into global trade networks, with few import restrictions and relatively low protective barriers.
Average tariff rates on affected goods were raised by about seven percentage points in 2018.

In the late 2010s, Papua New Guinea's tariff policy took a significant turn as a result of economic challenges. Facing economic headwinds such as foreign exchange shortages, fiscal pressures, and a push to develop domestic industries, the government began reconsidering its open trade stance. A notable precursor was a brief import ban on select fruits and vegetables from Australia in late 2015, an attempt to protect local farmers (Fox et al., 2018).

In August 2017, the government formally suspended the TRP before the final 2018 cuts could be implemented. Instead of reducing the remaining tariffs to 10 per cent as planned, Papua New Guinea moved to raise many tariffs in order to shelter domestic producers. In the 2018 Budget (enacted in late 2017), authorities announced increases on roughly 250 tariff lines and simultaneously scrapped or deferred over 600 scheduled tariff reductions. Average tariff rates on affected goods were raised by about seven percentage points in 2018. This policy reversal accelerated in the following year: by 2019, Papua New Guinea had introduced a total of 323
tariff line increases over two years, with an average hike of around 14 percentage points in the second round (Laveil, 2020).

Many of these changes targeted goods that compete with nascent or existing local industries, in line with the government's renewed emphasis on import substitution and industrialization. For example, a 25 per cent import duty on milk was imposed (milk had previously been duty-free) to support Papua New Guinea's first domestic dairy venture, Ilimo Dairy Farm. Tariffs on items like frozen meats, packaged fruits, sugar and confectionery, flour and cereals, certain textiles and apparel, furniture, and household goods (soaps, detergents, etc.) were also raised significantly. The highest tariffs faced were for tobacco products with an ad valorem equivalent (AVE) of 155 per cent, followed by 65 per cent for beverages, 34 per cent for edible vegetables, 27 per cent for meat and meat products, 26 per cent for pearls and diamonds, 23 per cent for sugars, 20 per cent for furniture and 20 per cent for coffee (See Figure 5). The Customs Tariff Amendment Act of 2018 explicitly stated its intent was to “provide relief to local pioneer industries and existing local manufacturers from cheap imports” (Laveil, 2020). In practice, this meant reinstating protective barriers for a range of products to give local businesses a price advantage over imports.

paragraph_content.content: This reversal of past policies marked a new protectionist chapter in Papua New Guinea's trade policy. After nearly two decades of falling tariffs, Papua New Guinea's rates on some goods began climbing for the first time since the late 1990s. The tariff schedule became more complex, with new 12.5 per cent, 20 per cent, and 25 per cent bands added. The change sparked debate. Proponents argued this protection would nurture infant industries such as dairy, poultry, and textiles. Critics noted mixed past results from similar policies: Ramu Sugar struggled for decades despite high protection, while Halla Cement only became competitive after privatisation and lower tariffs (Fox et al., 2018). Critics of the 2018–19 tariff hikes pointed to these, arguing that prolonged protection can lead to inefficiency and high consumer prices without guaranteeing a globally competitive industry (Laveil, 2020). They also warned that reversing the TRP could harm Papua New Guinea's export sectors, as higher tariffs raise input costs for Papua New Guinea's exporters and risk retaliatory measures or losing credibility in trade negotiations.
By 2020, the government signalled a pause on further tariff changes. The

2020 budget contained no new increases, but the protective measures remained in place with no further tariff reduced. As of the early 2020s, Papua New Guinea's applied tariff rates remained higher than the lows achieved under the TRP, especially for products deemed important to “import-replacement” industries. Papua New Guinea stayed within its WTO bindings, avoiding breaches, but the reversal marked a clear shift from the liberalisation path followed since 1999.

This evolution from aggressive tariff cuts in the early 2000s to consolidation and commitment to free trade agreements and then to a resurgence of protectionist measures highlights how economic conditions, government objectives, and international influences have continually reshaped Papua New Guinea's tariff landscape over the past twenty years. Each phase of the Tariff Reduction Programme and decisions to partial reverse changes were driven by a mix of economic rationale and political debate, underscoring the challenge of balancing development goals with global trade commitments in Papua New Guinea.

title_content.content: Government policies on trade and industry

paragraph_content.content: Papua New Guinea implemented several sectoral and horizontal plans to support industry and trade. While tariff policies are typically decided by a Ministry of Finance (or Treasury in the case of Papua New Guinea), their objectives are often multiple and span several policy domains. These may include raising government revenue to ensure fiscal sustainability, restricting products harmful to the environment, protecting emerging industries, supporting industrial or agricultural development, and addressing external imbalances. Because of these diverse objectives, coordination across government institutions with different mandates is therefore essential to ensure alignment with the various policies of the Government.

Tariff policy aligned with the goals of the Medium-Term Development Plan (MTDP) IV (2023–2027) to promote diversification. By raising tariffs on processed foods, textiles, wood products and consumer goods, the government created a price advantage for domestic firms engaged in downstream processing, in line with the MTDP IV's focus on job creation, SME promotion, and adding value to Papua New Guinea's natural resources before export.

Sectoral development plans in forestry, fisheries, agriculture, and industry also reveal the way tariff policy was integrated into the drive for diversification. High tariffs on wood and furniture, and the log export ban policy, supported local timber processing. In agriculture, tariffs on dairy, vegetables, and processed foods created space for new agribusiness ventures, while in fisheries, duties on canned and smoked fish reinforced incentives for local processing. While tariffs alone were not always sufficient to stimulate competitive industries, they formed part of a wider policy mix designed to encourage local value addition, support SMEs, and expand Papua New Guinea's industrial base.

Papua New Guinea's National Trade Policy (NTP) 2017–2032 marked a strategic shift in trade policy. At its launch in 2017, the government suspended the TRP. Furthermore, the government declared that Papua New Guinea would review all trade agreements and even consider suspending trade with partners seen as unfair, underscoring a more assertive, Papua New Guinea-first stance. Reflecting this stance, Papua New Guinea declined to join the Pacific Agreement on Closer Economic Relations Plus (PACER-Plus) regional free trade agreement. Instead seeking arrangements with Australia and
New Zealand that yield tangible investment, export earnings and jobs for Papua New Guineans (Post Courrier, 2017).

The subsequent tariff adjustments in 2018–2020 align with the NTP's protective orientation. According to the 2019 Customs Tariff Amendment Act, the rationale for recent tariff increases was “to provide relief to local pioneer industries and existing local manufacturers from cheap imports” (The National, 2020). In other words, the tariff policy has been reoriented to nurture domestic industries – a key goal of the NTP – by sheltering them from import competition.

title_content.content: B. Medium Term Development Plan IV (2023-2027)

paragraph_content.content: Papua New Guinea's MTDP IV embodies objectives that relate to trade and tariffs. The MTDP IV targets broad economic growth and explicitly aims to “encourage downstream processing of our natural resources” (Ministry of Treasury, 2024). This priority reflects a desire to add value locally in sectors like agriculture, forestry, fisheries and mining, rather than exporting raw commodities. The tariff adjustments support this goal by making certain imported finished goods relatively more expensive and thus giving an edge to local producers of processed foods, wood products, textiles, and other manufactures. For example, tariffs were raised on a range of food products and consumer goods, including frozen meats, packaged fruits and vegetables, sugar, confectionery, flour, garments, wood and paper products, furniture and others, which is consistent with incentivizing domestic processing in those product
chains. The MTDP IV also emphasizes job creation (one million additional jobs) and promotion of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (Fox et al., 2018).

However, the MTDP IV simultaneously calls for a “conducive environment to attract Foreign Direct Investment”. This implies that tariff policy must strike a balance, providing reasonable protection to encourage local production, while not creating an overly prohibitive or unpredictable trade regime that could deter investors. Excessive or ad hoc tariff increases could conflict with the objective of a stable, investment-friendly climate. This tension is recognized by policymakers; indeed, observers noted that Papua New Guinea’s abrupt deviation from the TRP in 2018 introduced new tariff rates (12.5, 20, 25 per cent) beyond the previous uniform structure and set a precedent for lobbying by industries for even higher tariffs (Fox et al., 2018).

Papua New Guinea's MTRS 2023–2027 provides another lens through which to view tariff policy. The MTRS seeks to halt the decline in revenue-to-GDP and raise it to about 17.9 per cent by 2027 through improved compliance and a broader tax base (Ministry of Treasury, 2024). It emphasizes shifting toward consumption-based taxes in a fair, efficient manner while minimizing ad-hoc exemptions.

Tariffs play a dual role in this strategy. On one hand, they provide revenue, and the increases in 2018–2019 (averaging 7 per cent and 14 per cent) offered short-term relief to a budget under strain (The National, 2020). On the other hand, the MTRS cautions against measures that undermine efficiency. Higher tariffs can discourage imports, reduce GST collections, or encourage smuggling if rates are excessive (The National, 2020).

The trade-off between revenue and efficiency is acknowledged by analysts – for example, an overvalued exchange rate was identified as a more direct cause of competitiveness issues, suggesting that devaluing the Kina would be a more efficient way to assist both import-competing and export sectors than raising tariffs (Fox et al., 2018).

Thus, to remain consistent with the MTRS, tariff policy should be carefully calibrated: providing needed revenue and industry support, but complemented by broader tax reforms and macroeconomic adjustments to ensure it does not undermine productivity or compliance.

paragraph_content.content: Under the European Union–Pacific EPA (and the United Kingdom–Pacific EPA), Papua New Guinea enjoys full duty-free, quota-free access for its exports to the European Union/United Kingdom, while committing to gradually liberalize 80–90 per cent of its own tariff lines over 15–25 years. The protective tariff measures taken in 2018–2020 do not necessarily violate the EPA, as the agreement allows asymmetric and gradual liberalization with safeguards for food security (WTO, 2019). Many sensitive items can be excluded or liberalized at a slower pace. However, the spirit of the EPA and similar agreements is toward lower tariffs in the long run. Thus, Papua New Guinea will need to ensure that its interim tariff hikes on industrial and consumer goods are consistent with its schedule of reductions under these agreements. For instance, if milk or furniture imports from the European Union were slated for tariff cuts under the EPA schedule, Papua New Guinea might have to reconcile the temporary hike with its eventual phase-down commitments. WTO-consistency and regional commitments, therefore, set important outer boundaries for Papua New Guinea's tariff policy.

In summary, the 2018–2020 tariff adjustments were formulated to advance national policy goals (industrial development, revenue, value addition) and are broadly aligned with those domestic plans. But Papua New Guinea also faces the task of managing these tariffs in harmony with its international obligations, honouring its WTO-bound rates and progressive liberalization under trade agreements, to maintain credibility and avoid penalties. So far, Papua New Guinea's actions (such as suspending the TRP and raising certain duties) have been taken unilaterally in pursuit of national interest, but going forward, a careful alignment with trade agreements will be essential to sustain an open yet development-friendly trade regime.

paragraph_content.content: Chapter 4

The relationship between Papua New Guinea's tariff policy evolution and broader economic performance is complex and requires a deeper dive to understand the underlying reasons for the outcomes obtained after tariff changes. For example, during the active TRP period, Papua New Guinea's economy exhibited remarkable growth at an average of 6.3 per cent annually. This growth slowed down during TRP-suspension period at 2.0 per cent (IMF, 2025). Using a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods, this chapters dive into the linkages between tariffs and trade performance, and examines multiple contributing factors, such as global commodity cycles and major investment projects. Insights from the business sector is also incorporated to give a sense about the practical implications of the tariff policy and how it could be better designed in combination with the larger public policy framework.

title_content.content: Analytical approach employed for the analysis

paragraph_content.content: To evaluate the outcomes and impacts of the TRP, the study relies on two complementary methodologies: an ex-post econometric analysis of trade flows, which assesses the results of the implementation of the TRP on specific economic variables, and an ex-ante partial equilibrium simulation, which assesses the expected changes to occur as a result of tariff changes. All analysis is based on data obtained from international data sets, namely from UN Comtrade, ITC TradeMap, ITC MacMap, and the World Bank WITS. This data was also compared to national data obtained from the Papua New Guinea Customs Service.

Partial equilibrium simulation (ex-ante projections): A partial equilibrium (PE) trade model was employed to simulate the impact of tariff changes on trade, welfare, and revenue. Two periods were examined: (1) TRP Implementation (2010–2018) – comparing outcomes with the tariff reductions against a counterfactual of no tariff change against the baseline (2010); and (2) TRP Suspension (2018–2023), comparing outcomes with the tariff increases against a counterfactual of retaining 2017 tariff rates, which were the lower tariffs. The model uses detailed import data by product and source country, along with import demand elasticities, to estimate how a tariff cut or hike would change import quantities, government tariff revenue, and welfare (measured by consumer surplus). For instance, for normal goods that exhibit a price elasticity, lowering a tariff should increase demand (and import volumes) but reduce per-unit tariff revenue. Raising a tariff would do the opposite, all else being equal. The results from the PE model quantify the effects on a product-by-product basis. Notably, the model captures the largest trading partners (like China and Australia) to see how their exports to Papua New Guinea were affected by tariff changes, and it computes the net welfare impact (consumer surplus change) for Papua New Guinea's consumers from each policy change.

Gravity modelling (ex-post analysis): A standard bilateral gravity model of trade was employed to quantify how changes in tariffs affected Papua New Guinea's import volumes. This model relates Papua New Guinea's observed import values to various factors: (i) the tariff level on each product, (ii) the economic size of trading partners, and (iii) trade frictions. In formal terms, for each HS-6 product and partner country, the specification regresses the log of import value on the applied tariff (trade-weighted average) and controls. The regression includes partner GDP (to capture market size), distance between

paragraph_content.content: Papua New Guinea and the partner (a proxy for transport cost), a dummy for whether the partner has a free trade agreement (FTA) with Papua New Guinea (e.g., Australia under PACER Plus, or other regional agreements), and a measure of the partner's regulatory quality (to proxy overall trade facilitation). Year fixed effects control for global shocks, and product-group fixed effects capture commodity-specific factors. This approach isolates the partial effect of tariff changes on imports, holding other factors constant. The gravity model estimation provides an elasticity of import demand with respect to tariff changes and indicates whether Papua New Guinea's recent tariff hikes or cuts significantly altered import behaviour.

A tariff comparison between 2010 and 2023 indicates a shift in Papua New Guinea's trade protection policies over time. In 2010, after the first phase of the TRP, ad valorem equivalent (AVE) tariffs were relatively high and more dispersed across various product groups, showing peaks in sectors associated with agriculture, textiles, and manufacturing. During the TRP and up to mid-2018, tariff decreases were witnessed for several products, such as sugar and confectionery products, furniture, while witnessing a jump in tariffs for beverages and tobacco products (Figure 7). Several other tariffs have fallen during the TRP, though few tariff eliminations have been witnessed. The 2010 tariffs had a wider spread, indicating high protection levels for certain goods, particularly in sectors where local industries required shielding from international competition.

In contrast, the 2023 AVE tariffs show a more selective protectionist approach, with some tariffs significantly increased while others remain low. The tariff peaks in 2023 suggest renewed protection for specific industries, reflecting Papua New Guinea's post-2018 shift toward import substitution and infant industry protection (Figure 8). The higher tariffs in key sectors indicate targeted intervention rather than across-the-board tariff reductions. This change aligns with Papua New Guinea's suspension of TRP in 2018 and the subsequent introduction of higher tariffs on select products in the 2018–2020 budgets. The overall trend suggests that Papua New Guinea, after years of liberalization,

has partially reversed its approach, likely to support domestic industries and reduce dependence on imports, but with potential trade-offs such as higher consumer prices and limited international competitiveness in protected sectors.

Despite the rationalization of tariffs between 2010 and 2023, Papua New Guinea's protective measures continued to disproportionately affect more raw materials and continued to be applied to intermediate products. Grouping up the tariffs according to the product types, whether raw material, intermediary inputs to industry, consumer goods or capital goods, allows one to reflect on the levels of protection applied to strategic inputs into industry or to import competing industries. During the TRP (2012-2017), all tariff categories decreased. Raw materials dropped from 11.4 to 10.8 per cent, consumer goods from 6.4 to 5.2 per cent, intermediate goods from 2 to 1.5 per cent, and capital goods from 0.3 to 0.1 per cent. After the suspension of the TRP (2018-2023), most tariffs bounced back up, but only in a moderate fashion. Tariff protection on raw materials rose to 11.3 per cent, from 10.8 per cent in 2017, while tariffs on consumer goods rose from 4.9 (at their lowest point in 2018) to 5.3 per cent in 2023. Intermediate goods stayed steady at between 1.5-1.7 per cent on average, though the changes are still surprising from year to year. Finally, tariffs on capital goods remained very low, ranging between an average of 0.1 and 0.2 per cent (Figure 9).

paragraph_content.content: The distribution of tariff levels across categories of products affects raw materials, consumer products and intermediary products most. From the baseline in 2010 to the last year of the TRP's implementation in 2017, the distribution of tariffs has been rationalized, and average tariffs dropped. The fewer differences in rates of tariffs (indicated by blue dots in Figure 11) across the scale suggest a simplification of the tariff schedule. This is especially true for consumer products. When it comes to the TRP suspension period, it starts off in 2018 with a major increase in complexity and variability of rates across all types of products. The increase in intermediary products and raw materials is surprising from the perspective of simplifying and facilitating businesses engaged in trade. By 2023, the complex structure observed in 2018 had reversed, resulting once again in a more simplified and rationalized tariff schedule.

The distribution of tariff levels across Harmonized system (HS) codes has also varied and become less scattered over time during and after the suspension of the TRP. In particular, in 2010, there was a high dispersion of tariffs along HS2 clusters, with many products facing a 20 to 40 per cent tariff rate. In some cases, there were tariffs applied at a 60 per cent tariff in ad valorem terms. By 2018, the dispersion of tariffs along HS clusters fell, with the distance between tariff rates compressing. Most products also faced a far lower tariff rate of below 20 per cent. This reduction in dispersion is clearly visible in HS chapters such as HS17 and HS94, which show a much narrower range of tariff rates in 2018 compared to 2010. In particular, tariffs under HS94 exceeded 40 per cent in 2010 but fell below that level in subsequent years. By 2023, during the suspension of the TRP, some tariffs rose, but the pattern of dispersion along HS clusters was remarkably similar to that witnessed in 2018 (Figure 12).

The survey conducted for this study asked business respondents whether the nature of tariff revisions between 2018 and 2020 had any impact on their investment decisions. The results provide a clear indication that tariff uncertainty significantly influenced strategic planning for a majority of businesses. Out of the total respondents, 61 per cent reported that ad-hoc tariff changes directly affected their investment decisions. This indicates that most firms felt compelled to either delay, modify, or reconsider their investment plans in response to an unstable trade policy environment. Such findings highlight the disruptive role of

title_content.content: B. Economic outcomes and sector performance

paragraph_content.content: Trade trends in Papua New Guinea suggest a robust growth in exports and a decline in imports between 2010 to 2024. Imports declined significantly, from a high of $8 billion in 2012, despite the gradual tariff reductions. At the same time, exports increased steadily, driven by strong performance in resource sectors like mining, oil, and gas. The trade balance for Papua New Guinea has overall remained positive over this period, with a slight dip in 2012, but improved sharply

afterwards as exports surged (Figure 13). The factors behind the improved performance in the trade balance reflect less the tariff policy and more other external factors, including the thriving mining sector. Following the suspension of TRP in 2018, import levels remained subdued, likely due to the introduction of higher protective tariffs and import substitution policies. Meanwhile, exports peaked in 2022, benefiting from high global commodity prices and the expansion of exports from extractive industries.

title_content.content: A number of factors explain why Papua New Guinea's imports fell during 2012–2017 despite tariff cuts.

paragraph_content.content: One likely factor was broader economic conditions: Papua New Guinea was completing a large LNG investment project around 2014 and then faced a downturn in commodity prices, which constrained foreign exchange and import capacity. Thus, the macro environment dominated the tariff effect, masking any import-stimulating impact that lower tariffs would typically have. Additionally, Papua New Guinea maintained zero tariffs on a large share of essentials even before TRP, therefore cutting tariffs mainly affected other goods whose demand might be price-elastic but subject to income constraints.
During the active TRP period, Papua New Guinea's economy exhibited remarkable growth at an average 6.3 per cent annually. This performance stands in stark contrast to the post-

suspension period, which saw average growth rates decline to 2.0 per cent (Figure 14). While correlation does not equal causation, the timing and magnitude of economic changes during different policy phases provide important insights into the role of trade openness in small island economies. Furthermore, multiple factors contributed to the differential trends, including global commodity cycles and major resource project developments (for the TRP Phase under investigation), as well as the COVID-19 outbreak (for the TRP Suspension), necessitating careful interpretation of the correlation with trade policy phases. Papua New Guinea's external position, measured through the current account balance, has remained consistently strong. The balance has been positive since 2014 and has exceeded 10 per cent of GDP for the entire decade for which data are available.

paragraph_content.content: The gravity model analysis shows that tariffs do have a negative relationship with import volumes, but the elasticity is modest. Specifically, a 1 per cent increase in tariffs (ad valorem) is associated with a 2.1 per cent decrease in import value on average, holding other factors constant (see details in Annex 3). This implies that Papua New Guinea's import demand is somewhat price-sensitive, but this effect can be overshadowed by other forces. The results from the gravity model further suggest that tariff increases have a more significant effect in dampening the demand for importing raw materials and consumables. On the other hand, tariffs had little measured impact on intermediate goods imports, possibly because industries had no close substitutes for those inputs. For capital goods, the model found a positive correlation with tariffs, which is not causal but rather reflects that many capital goods imports in Papua New Guinea enjoy duty exemptions (for priority infrastructure or investment projects). This finding aligns with the practice of exempting crucial imports; for example, mining equipment or electricity generators might be exempted, meaning tariff hikes do not reduce those imports.

Import composition showed a strong shift towards consumer goods during the liberalization period. From 2012 to 2017, the share of consumer goods in total imports increased from 28 per cent to 41 per cent during the TRP, eventually reaching 46 per cent by 2023 (Figure 16). This structural change reflects both the direct effects of tariff reductions on consumer goods and the indirect effects of improved purchasing power driving consumption growth. The rising share of consumer goods imports could reflect increased demand for foreign consumer products as tariffs

fell and Papua New Guinea's purchasing power grew modestly. It might also indicate that local manufacturing did not expand to meet consumer needs, so imports filled the gap over time. Intermediate goods showed a gradual expansion from an average 12.5 per cent share during the TRP to 16 per cent following the suspension of the TRP, indicating continued dependence on imported inputs for domestic production processes. On the other hand, raw material imports experienced the opposite trend, with their share in total imports halving from 13 per cent to 7 per cent during the TRP and remaining at these low levels after suspending the TRP (Figure 16). The decline in raw material imports could be due to the expansion of Papua New Guinea's agriculture and resource sectors to supply more raw inputs locally, or due to the stagnating manufacturing (which uses raw materials) which required fewer imported inputs.

In value terms, despite liberalization measures, all import categories actually contracted during the TRP (2012-2017). Raw materials declined at a rapid annual rate of 19.4 per cent, and capital goods fell 15.2 per cent annually. The post-suspension period from 2018 to 2023 witnessed recovery in three of four major import categories, with consumer goods leading strongly at an 8.1 per cent compound annual growth rate. Raw materials continued their decline at 4.1 per cent annually, possibly correlating with the increase in tariffs following the TRP suspension. On the other hand, both intermediate goods and capital goods returned to modest positive growth (Figure 17). These patterns may suggest that the earlier contraction reflected temporary factors such as major project completions and exchange rate adjustments rather than fundamental structural changes driven by tariff policy.

paragraph_content.content: Examination of agriculture, mining, and manufacturing performance, using the gross value added (GVA) index over the past two decades, reveals that the tariff policy alone did not generate much change to the performance of major sectors of the economy. Agriculture exhibited steady, gradual growth throughout the entire period. Even when tariffs fell sharply under the TRP, Papua New Guinea's agriculture, forestry, and fishing sector maintained output expansion, though at a slow rate (Figure 18). This indicated that exposure to global competition did not cripple farmers; on the contrary, agricultural growth was “steady” and resilient. Mining and quarrying showed a different pattern: an initial dip around 2010–2012, followed by a significant surge from 2014 to 2019.

This boom was more likely to correspond to new resource projects (like the LNG project commencing in 2014) and high commodity prices rather than any tariff policy effect, as Papua New Guinea mining is largely an export sector with little reliance on import protection. Manufacturing, covering sectors such as agro-processing and light industry, clearly underperformed, with GVA revealing to be almost flat or declining throughout both the TRP and TRP suspension phases, making it the slowest-growing sector. Notably, even after 2017, when tariffs were raised, the manufacturing index was constantly below the 2010 level and only inched upward modestly by 2022, implying that protection gave limited relief. Furthermore, the stagnation reflects Papua New Guinea's ongoing struggle to develop its manufacturing base.

paragraph_content.content: The above evidence suggests that tariff liberalization did not affect agriculture, as the sector continued to grow – possibly benefiting from cheaper imported farm inputs like machinery or fertilizer, and facing little direct competition since Papua New Guinea’s agriculture is oriented around crops which were not heavily imported, such as coffee, cocoa, and palm oil. Manufacturing, however, saw virtually no growth when tariffs were low, which may have reinforced the perceptions that it needed protection. However, it is important to note that Papua New Guinea's manufacturing faced small-scale and high-cost (energy, transport, and logistics, see Figure 27), which, even with tariffs, made it hard for local manufacturers to compete with lower-priced imports.

paragraph_content.content: The sector's struggles during liberalization suggest that tariff policy alone cannot overcome fundamental structural constraints that limit manufacturing development in Papua New Guinea's economic context.

The results from the partial equilibrium model estimation show limited effects of tariffs on Papua New Guinea's trade with partners. China and Australia are the most affected markets, due to the size of trade with these markets, although the change in tariffs (both during the TRP and after the TRP suspension) only caused a single-digit million-dollar change in imports for both partners (Table 3). Between 2010-2018, the reduction in tariffs led to a simulated $7 million more imports from China and $2.7 million more from Australia. Between 2018–2023, the tariff rise led to a simulated $6.8 million less imports from China. In contrast, Australia benefited from a tariff reduction during the Papua New Guinea TRP suspension, which is simulated to have resulted in an increase of $4.5 million in imports from Australia. These small changes can be explained by the number and volume of imports affected by tariff changes during and after the TRP for Papua New Guinea's major trade partners (Table 4 and Table 5).

paragraph_content.content: A critical aspect of tariff policy is its impact on government revenue. The tax-to-GDP ratio in Papua New Guinea has fallen between 2010 and 2023, reaching 15.8 per cent in 2023 (Figure 19). During the same period, tax revenue has increased from around 6.6 billion PGK in 2010 to 17.6 billion PGK in 2023. This apparent divergence reflects the faster expansion of nominal GDP relative to tax collections. Import duties have long been an important source of fiscal revenue for Papua New

Guinea, though their share in total tax collected has declined with the introduction of GST and tax reforms. Nevertheless, according to the OECD (2025), total tax collected by customs and import duties rose from 189 million PGK in 2010 to 403 million PGK in 2023 (Figure 20). While fiscal revenues increased in absolute terms, there was an observed marginal decline in relative terms during the TRP and an increase during the suspension, followed by a decline in 2023 to its lowest level.

paragraph_content.content: The analysis of tariff revenue by product category revealed that consumer goods produced the bulk of Papua New Guinea's tariff revenue. The fact that consumer products generate most revenue (Figure 21) is not surprising since consumer goods (e.g. fuel, vehicles, alcohol, tobacco, processed foods) have both high tariff rates and substantial import volumes. Intermediate goods and raw materials often have lower tariffs and/or low import quantities, contributing relatively little to fiscal revenue collection. The data showed that even though raw materials had high nominal tariffs in some cases, they generate minimal government revenue because import volumes are so low. In contrast, consumer goods – even with moderate tariffs – generated a lot of revenue due to the sheer volume of imports. For example, fuels (HS27) have AVE tariff rates of between 0 per cent to 0.5 per cent, yet the level of imports was $751 million in 2018, generating large absolute values of revenue.

This suggests that there is little policy space for attempting to increase revenue by raising tariffs on other product categories, such as raw materials (due to the low volumes of imports), and raising tariffs further on consumer goods runs into the risk of lowering volumes of imports or incentivizing under-reporting, under-invoicing, or potentially attempting to evade duties. Any additional attempts to raise revenue may hit diminishing returns. Moreover, Papua New Guinea's Medium Term Revenue Strategy (2023–2027) emphasizes improving tax collection and diversifying revenue sources. The

evidence suggests that trade taxes are a limited tool for revenue generation. Imports can contribute to fiscal revenue, but usually through the imposition of GST most directly, while expansion of the economy will lead to higher income tax, corporate tax and GST collection through the expansion of spending.

Lowering tariff rates may reduce tariff revenue collection or increase it, depending on the elasticities of demand. Despite the evidence, holding all factors constant, it is interesting to simulate the expected changes in revenue from tariff changes. During the TRP, as tariff rates declined, revenue from import duties would be expected to drop proportionally. Using the partial equilibrium model, the modelled results estimate that tariff revenue in 2010–2018 would decline only marginally, holding flows of trade constant. Specifically, the partial equilibrium simulation estimated that the tariff reductions under TRP caused about a $7.8 million annual revenue loss by 2018, relative to what revenue would have been without those cuts. To put this in context, this would present a shortfall in just over 1 per cent of tariff revenue collected, almost insignificant in terms of the overall fiscal revenue stream. This small impact is because many of Papua New Guinea's imports were either zero-rated already or not strongly affected by slight tariff changes (especially given import contraction in those years). Additionally, the GST in Papua New Guinea applies to imports, so as tariffs fell, GST collected on a possibly higher import base could offset some losses (Figure 22).

paragraph_content.content: After 2018, with the TRP suspension, the expectation was that fiscal revenue would increase when tariffs rise. On a static basis, higher rates on the same import volume should yield more revenue.

However, two dynamic effects played out: volume reductions (imports of some items fell because of higher prices) and policy reversals on specific items. The simulation for 2018–2023 shows a somewhat surprising result: tariff revenues were about \$15.6 million lower with the post-2018 tariff increases than they would have been if Papua New Guinea had maintained its baseline 2018 levels of tariffs. In other words, raising tariffs did not raise revenue. A deep dive into the results reveals the

primary reason for this outcome: Papua New Guinea slashed the tariff rate on tobacco soon after raising other tariffs. Tobacco is a top revenue-generating import (due to high volume and previously very high rates), so when its duty was reduced from 159 per cent to 58 per cent, the government forewent a huge amount of potential revenue on that item. Essentially, Papua New Guinea suspended the TRP “to gain revenue,” but then undermined that goal by cutting taxes on one of its most fiscal generating tariff lines (Figure 22).
Overall, tariff liberalization cost Papua New Guinea little in forgone revenue, while the attempt to reverse it did not yield the expected revenue gains. A

It is possible that higher tariffs encouraged more evasion or smuggling, meaning the import volumes reported (and taxed) declined disproportionately. title_content.content: D. Industry perspectives and cross cutting observations

paragraph_content.content: Industry views paint a complex picture of competitive challenges that are informative for trade policy considerations. During the liberalization period from 2012 to 2017, while 55 per cent of surveyed firms reported no benefits, 36 per cent of firms reported some benefits from tariff reductions, primarily through lower costs for imported inputs, capital goods, and equipment. These cost savings enabled some businesses to reduce sales prices,

expand operations, or invest in productivity improvements (Figure 23). Following the tariff increases since 2018, 53 per cent of surveyed businesses reported negative effects, while only 8 per cent reported positive impacts (Figure 24). This suggests that policy volatility creates potential winners and losers within the business community, and negative impacts are more easily felt than benefits, further necessitating scrutiny in designing trade policy measures.

Several structural challenges were shown as major hurdles for domestic production capacity and competitiveness. According to the survey results, transport and logistics costs emerged as overwhelming challenges for business operations, with 94 per cent of survey respondents rating these factors as high or very high barriers to competitiveness. This near-universal concern reflects Papua New Guinea's fundamental geographic challenges, including its archipelagic geography, mountainous terrain, and underdeveloped infrastructure networks.

For many businesses, the cost of moving products within Papua New Guinea or connecting to international markets exceeds the impact of tariff policy changes by orders of magnitude. The survey further revealed what can be characterized as a “triple impact” affecting business operations beyond transport challenges, namely expensive imported inputs, unpredictable policies, and regulatory burdens. Specifically, 76 per cent of respondents identified expensive imported inputs as a significant operational barrier, while 73 per cent and 59 per cent cited policy

trade policy should be accompanied by an enabling, predictable regulatory environment and well-suited infrastructure to support businesses in productivity and competition capacity improvement.

paragraph_content.content: During the TRP years, Papua New Guinea's more open trade regime coincided with what can be described as an export product “boom”. Data on the extensive margin of trade (the number of distinct products exported) show a clear uptick, suggesting that firms, enjoying lower input costs and easier access to imported equipment and materials, started venturing into new product lines for export. In the 2010-2018 period, 591 new products entered Papua New Guinea's export portfolio, representing 45 per cent of the total export basket (Figure 28). Most of the new products were of very little value (under $100,000 in 2018). Only 44 products exceeding $100,000 in exports in 2018 were new products in comparison to 2010 (see Annex 4 for the list of products). This increase in product innovation suggests that lower input costs enabled domestic firms to test international markets and explore new competitive opportunities. However, export sustainability proved challenging,

with only 465 products (35 per cent of the total) surviving the full TRP period. The figure indicates that cost advantages from input tariff reductions, while helpful for market entry, proved insufficient for sustained international competitiveness without addressing broader structural constraints affecting Papua New Guinea's productive capacity. On the other hand, the post-TRP period revealed the fragility of these export gains, with 494 products disappearing from Papua New Guinea's export portfolio (36 per cent of the total) while only 325 new products emerged (23 per cent). This pattern demonstrates how tariff increases can have unintended negative consequences for export competitiveness, particularly in sectors requiring imported intermediate goods or specialized equipment.

One key observation during the TRP was its association with export diversification and an entrepreneurial response by Papua New Guinea's private sector, followed by a setback once tariffs were raised.

paragraph_content.content: The observed boom-and-bust pattern in export diversification is telling. Under the TRP, companies likely took advantage of cheaper imported inputs, intermediate goods, and capital machinery to venture into processing or manufacturing new products. Lower tariffs likely made imported inputs (materials, components) more affordable, thus reducing production costs for potential export industries. Furthermore, an open import regime can help exports because exporters often need imported machinery and raw materials to produce goods that

meet international standards. Additionally, the TRP signalled a commitment to open trade, possibly encouraging investment (domestic or foreign) in new ventures oriented towards export markets, knowing that inputs could be sourced at world prices. After 2018, the reversal in policy (i.e., higher tariffs) likely increased costs for those budding industries.
Firm-level behaviour and perceptions offer insights into how trade policy affected business decisions in the innovation area. Results from

paragraph_content.content: the business survey reflect how firms perceived the impact of tariff changes on investment and innovation. Specifically, 46 per cent of surveyed firms reported launching a new product or export in the last five years. This suggests a strong entrepreneurial drive (Figure 29). But

many also reported that higher input costs, equipment import restrictions, and constant policy changes made product development more difficult and expensive. This further emphasizes the roles of stable policy for investors' confidence and business innovation capacity.

paragraph_content.content: Trade policy has direct consequences for consumer welfare through its impact on prices and product availability. The welfare effects of the TRP can be assessed using consumer surplus, a measure of the benefit consumers obtain from being able to purchase goods at certain prices, derived from partial equilibrium simulations. In theory, consumer welfare outcomes depend on the balance between short-term price pressures caused by tariffs and the longer-terms domestic industry development. In the short term, higher tariffs on finished products could lead to an increase in consumer prices for imported goods, thus reducing purchasing power, especially for lower income groups. Over the longer term, consumers may benefit from improved access to locally produced substitutes if protective tariffs succeed in stimulating domestic industries, they could

contribute to price stabilization, fostering import substitution, and strengthening local manufacturing capacity, thereby reducing dependence on expensive imports. However, there is also a risk that reduced competition from imports may limit product variety and quality in the domestic market, particularly if domestic industries do not simultaneously improve their production standards and capabilities.

The consumer welfare impact of the tariff policies was heavily impacted by the radical change in a few product groups. During the Papua New Guinea TRP implementation period (2010–2018), one would expect consumer welfare to improve because tariffs coming down should lower prices. Indeed, many categories of consumer goods did see tariff reductions (the average tariff on consumer goods

page_header_content.content: Review of the Papua New Guinea Tariff Reduction Programme

paragraph_content.content: fell from ~23 per cent to ~14 per cent). However, the simulation results show a net welfare loss of around $5.9 million for Papua New Guinea consumers in this period (Figure 30). This seemingly paradoxical outcome can be explained by the structure of the tariff changes. While hundreds of products had small tariff cuts, a few products retained very high tariffs, which resulted in large negative effects. Specifically, throughout the TRP, Papua New Guinea kept high tariffs on beverages (alcohol, soft drinks) and tobacco. The welfare analysis indicates that this single policy (high tariffs on alcohol and tobacco) caused an estimated $6.5 million loss in consumer surplus. Beyond beverages and tobacco products, Papua New Guinea increased tariffs on about $390 million of other goods, lifting average rates from 5 per cent to 14 per cent, which contributed to a welfare loss of $1 million. The total consumer welfare loss, therefore, outweighed the $1.6 million gain consumers enjoyed from all the other tariff reductions. This finding is a reminder of the need for consideration of tariff impacts on items of common consumption or high expenditure with overall consumer welfare impact.
